job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Review: S. 2817, Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act (as amended October 6, 2026)

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), production threshold.** The 10,000-metric-ton-per-year trigger applies only to a "single vessel," so a company or consortium could run several vessels that each stay below the threshold, or split recovery across affiliated entities.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), depth and resource terms.** "Depths greater than 200 meters" does not say whether it refers to water depth or the depth of recovery, and "other mineral resources" is undefined. The text also does not clarify whether sub-seabed recovery (such as crusts or sulfides) is covered.

3. **Sec. 2(1), "commercial."** The definition never says what makes mining "commercial" (sale, intent to profit, or volume). Recovery framed as research or testing could fall outside it.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(B), discretionary determination.** The Secretary is not identified, and the bill gives no criteria, procedure, notice, or record for the "comparable risk" determination. This invites both non-action and a challenge that the determination was arbitrary.

5. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person."** Limiting the term to citizens and State-chartered corporations leaves out foreign-incorporated subsidiaries, LLCs, partnerships, and trusts, which weakens the "anywhere" reach in Sec. 3(a).

6. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel."** "Equipped for the recovery" is undefined, and vessels at or under 5,000 gross tons fall outside the registry in Sec. 4 entirely. A vessel can also be modified to fall under the threshold.

7. **Sec. 2 and Sec. 4, undefined terms.** "Person," "operator," "seabed," "exploration," and "recovery" are not defined. "Operator" matters most because Sec. 4 imposes duties on it.

8. **Sec. 3(a), jurisdictional reach.** "In the United States" does not specify whether it covers the territorial sea, the EEZ, or the outer continental shelf. Foreign persons mining in those zones, or non-U.S. persons mining beyond national jurisdiction, may fall outside the prohibition.

9. **Sec. 3(a), prohibited conduct.** "Engage in" is undefined. The bill does not say whether financing, equipment supply, ore processing, or vessel support count as engaging in mining.

10. **Sec. 3(b), grandfathering.** The bill does not identify the issuing authority for the "exploration license," and "mining conducted under" an exploration license could be read to allow commercial recovery. There are also no limits on renewal, transfer, volume, or duration.

11. **Sec. 3(b), heading mismatch.** The heading says "existing operations," but the text covers licenses. Operations begun without a license are not addressed.

12. **Sec. 3(c), environmental assessment exemption.** "Environmental assessment" is undefined, and the exemption has no limits on volume, duration, or permit requirements. Commercial-scale recovery could be labeled assessment and proceed without oversight.

13. **Sec. 4, no enforcement for registry or reporting.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register under Sec. 4(a) or to file under Sec. 4(b) carries no stated penalty.

14. **Sec. 4(b), report content and verification.** The bill sets no deadline, required content (tonnage, location, depth), public availability, or audit. Self-certification without verification makes the reports hard to rely on.

15. **Sec. 5(a) and Sec. 8, conflicting effective dates.** Sec. 5(a) applies penalties to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but Sec. 8 delays the Act's effect for 180 days, leaving unclear whether the prohibition is enforceable before then.

16. **Sec. 5(a), penalty calculation.** Counting penalties per day invites disputes over whether a violation is continuing or discrete. The bill does not address vessel-level liability, forfeiture of vessels or equipment, or injunctive relief.

17. **Sec. 5, enforcement authority.** The bill does not name the agency that investigates, assesses, or litigates violations, or say whether penalties are imposed administratively or only through courts.

18. **Sec. 5(b), criminal liability.** "Willfully" is undefined, and the bill does not address liability for corporate officers or directors.

19. **Sec. 6, international agreement.** "Shall seek to negotiate" creates no obligation to reach an agreement and no reporting requirement if none is reached. The bill also does not say whether a future agreement would change domestic obligations.

20. **Sec. 7(a), joint resolution standard.** "Serious harm" is undefined. The bill does not require the National Academies to report by any deadline, and it does not say what happens if no report is issued. A joint resolution could also be vetoed, so it is unclear whether the "finds" condition has been met.

21. **Sec. 7(a) and Sec. 7(b), internal conflict.** Sec. 7(a) makes the prohibition last until Congress acts, while Sec. 7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years. The bill does not say whether pending enforcement actions or violations committed during the 10 years survive the sunset.

22. **Missing general provisions.** The bill has no severability clause, no savings clause, no rulemaking authority, no judicial review provision, no authorization of appropriations, and no statement of its relationship to existing law.

---

**Items to verify before Thursday:**

- **Existing law.** The Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980 (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.) likely governs US-licensed seabed mining and may be what Sec. 3(b)'s "exploration license" refers to. Staff should confirm how S. 2817 interacts with it, and whether it has been amended.
- **International context.** Check the current status of the International Seabed Authority's mining code negotiations before relying on any statement about the Area beyond national jurisdiction.
- **Amendment history.** I reviewed only the text provided. I did not compare it with the prior version, so some drafting problems may already have been addressed or introduced by the October 6 manager's amendment.
- **Legislative counsel.** Some items above may be intentional policy choices rather than drafting errors. Confirm with committee staff or Legislative Counsel before presenting any item as a flaw.
